sections.heading: Dialogue I, Knot ii, part 2 (printed pp. 17–24)
rows: [p. 17] [Margin: Argumenta pro infinito solvuntur.] Andab. Non tam facile quam credis confectum est negotium. Non enim hoc aio, contradictionem in natura infiniti involvi: sed cum invictis rationibus constet possibilem esse infiniti rationem, tum demum hoc contendo, non parem esse cum finitis, sed hoc habere praecipui ut partes ipsius indeterminate sese habeant ad invicem, cum finiti partes determinato situ et distantia collocentur.

[p. 17] [Margin: Arguments for the infinite are resolved [solvuntur].] Andab. Not so easily as you believe has the business been made out [confectum est]. For I do not say this, that a contradiction is involved in the nature of the infinite: but since it is established [constet] by unconquered reasons [rationibus] that the reason [ratio] of the infinite is possible, then at last I contend this, that it is not equal [parem] with finite [things], but has this as [its] special [feature] [praecipui], that its parts hold themselves [sese habeant] indeterminately to one another, whereas [cum] the parts of the finite are placed in a determinate situation [situ] and distance.

Et ne videar verbis et ostentatione me defendere, committo me arenae. Hoc ergo imprimis assumo, possibile id dici, quo posito nihil inconveniens consequatur. Hoc axioma, Aristotelis et unanimi Logicorum consensu stabilitum est. Par, si non evidentius, adiungo aliud: posse unumquemque quantum potest: et ex his suadeo. Cum negari non possit Deum creare posse quantitatem quantam maximam potest, tanta quantitas non est impossibilis: Ponatur itaque, si quidem nullum inconveniens ex possibili sequitur. Sed talis quantitatis posita [p. 18] evidenter est infinita; Nihil itaque manifestius est quam infinitam magnitudinem esse possibilem.

And lest I seem to defend myself with words and ostentation, I commit myself to the arena. This therefore I assume [assumo] first of all: that that is said [to be] possible which, being posited, nothing inconvenient [inconveniens] follows. This axiom has been established by the consent of Aristotle and the unanimous [consent] of the Logicians. [An axiom] equal, if not more evident, I join [as] another: that each one can [do] as much as he can [posse unumquemque quantum potest]: and from these I persuade [suadeo]. Since it cannot be denied that God can create a quantity as great as the greatest [He] can [quantam maximam potest], so great a quantity is not impossible: Let it be posited [ponatur] therefore, since indeed no inconvenient [thing] follows from a possible. But [the magnitude] of such a quantity, posited, is [p. 18] evidently infinite; Nothing therefore is more manifest than that an infinite magnitude is possible.

Vides Ereuni ex quam manifestis et notissimis totum discursum fabricavi. Neque dissimilis est alia demonstratio: cum enim impossibilitas ex iis arguitur quae de re dicuntur, clarissimum est, quod impossibile est idem non esse intelligibile; si itaque convicero intelligi posse infinitum, effecero etiam possibile.

You see, Ereunius, out of how manifest and most known [things] I have fabricated the whole discourse [discursum]. Nor is the other demonstration dissimilar: for since impossibility is argued from those things which are said about the thing, it is most clear that what is impossible, the same [idem] is not intelligible; if therefore I shall have proved [convicero] that the infinite can be understood, I shall have made [it] also possible.

Quid ergo? Deus, et si quae creaturae omnes magnitudinis species, intelligit, num infinitas non intelligunt? Etsi infinitas, non unam aliquam ex sese infinitam? In primis enim omnes in unam colligant, et quoniam infinitae sunt, unam infinitam constituent. Rursus non quamlibet pertransierunt finitam? Et, si hoc in confesso sit, quae impudentia est negare eos aliquam infinitam cognoscere? si enim omnes finitas pertransierunt, infinitas pertransierunt uno v.g. [verbi gratia] passu sese invicem excedentes. Si ergo solos excessus colligamus, ex infinitis passibus collectio erit conflata.

What then? God, and any creatures if [there are such] [si quae creaturae], understands all the species [species] of magnitude; do they not then [num] understand infinite [species]? And if infinite, not some one [species] infinite of itself [ex sese]? For first of all let them gather [colligant] all into one, and since they are infinite, they will constitute one infinite. Again, have they not passed through [pertransierunt] any finite [one] you please? And, if this be among [things] confessed [in confesso], what impudence is it to deny that they know some infinite [one]? For if they have passed through all finite [ones], they have passed through infinite [ones] exceeding one another by, e.g. [v.g. = verbi gratia], one pace. If therefore we gather the excesses alone, a collection will have been blown together [conflata] from infinite paces.

Tandem sic accipe. Nulla est finita qua maiorem non cognoscant, singulis itaque finitis maiorem cognoscunt; sed singulae finitae in cumulo omnes efficiunt, omnibus itaque finitis aliquam maiorem sciunt; sed quae finitas omnes excedit, ipso hoc infinita est; infinitam itaque cognoscunt: intelligibilis proinde est infini-[p. 19]ta quantitas, neque impossibilis. Quid ad haec dicere habes cur non perfectissimae sint demonstrationes, et apertissime conclusum infiniti naturam non esse commentitiam?

Lastly, take [it] thus. There is no finite [one] than which they do not know a greater; therefore they know a greater [one] than each [singulis, dative] finite [one]; but the single finite [ones] in a heap [cumulo] make all; therefore they know some [one] greater than all finite [ones]; but what exceeds all finite [ones], by this very [fact] is infinite; therefore they know an infinite [one]: intelligible accordingly is an infini-[p. 19]te quantity, nor [is it] impossible. What have you to say to these [things], why the demonstrations are not most perfect, and [why it is not] most openly concluded that the nature of the infinite is not fictitious [commentitiam]?

Ereu. Ego vero ni ingenium tuum et acutissimam disputationem exosculer, haud ingenuus sim. Sed hoc attende, obsecro, unde hauseris quod manifestae veritati opponeres, et unde calumniam naturae ipsi moveres? Monstrata est infiniti ratio huic notissimo rationis principio, quo singulare sub universali subsumitur, repugnare? Tu ad Dei scientiam et potentiam convolasti, necessitatem effringendi rationis firmissima dictamina inde periturus.

Ereu. I indeed, unless I should fondly kiss [exosculer] your wit [ingenium] and most acute disputation, would hardly be ingenuous [ingenuus]. But attend to this, I beseech, whence you have drawn [hauseris] what you would oppose to manifest truth, and whence you would move a calumny against nature itself? Has the reason [ratio] of the infinite been shown to be repugnant to this most known principle of reason [rationis principio], by which the singular is subsumed under the universal? You have flown [convolasti] to the science [scientiam] and power [potentiam] of God, about to seek [periturus, read petiturus] thence the necessity of breaking open the firmest dictates of reason.

Haec autem, quam supra nos, quam ignota, quam admiranda magis quam investiganda sint tute rectissime intelligis. Qui autem ab ignoto petit unde notum impugnat, negotium facessat facile, aegre persuadeat.

But these [things]—how [far] above us, how unknown, how much more to be admired than to be investigated they are—you yourself [tute] most rightly understand. But he who seeks from the unknown [that] whence he attacks the known, may easily make trouble [negotium facessat], [but] would hardly [aegre] persuade.

Sed ut ad suasiones tuas cominus depugnem, scito evidentissimum illud tuum axioma, quo prima suasio nititur, aequivocum esse, et ex uno intellectu in alium insensibiliter te delabi. Illud dico quo asseris nihil notius, quam Deum posse creare quantitatem, quantum maximam potest creare. Cum enim creanda quantitas duos status habeat unum in potentia creantis, alium in ipsa se, exurgunt dicti huius tres explicationes.

But that I may fight [it] out [depugnem] at close quarters [cominus] against your persuasions [suasiones], know that that most evident axiom of yours, on which the first persuasion leans, is equivocal [aequivocum], and that you slip down insensibly from one understanding [intellectu] into another. I mean that by which you assert [that] nothing [is] more known than that God can create quantity as much the greatest as [quantum maximam] He can create. For since the quantity to be created has two states [status], one in the potency [potentia] of the [one] creating, another in itself, there rise up [exurgunt] three explications of this saying.

Prima, Deum in potentia sua tan-[p. 20]tam magnitudinem continere quantam in sua potentia continet, et in hac utrimque idem status rei in potentia designatur, estque propositio identica. Proxima explicatio est, eam quantitatem (si qua talis est) quae maxima a Deo in rerum natura existentiam habere potest, eam ab ipso maximam existere posse, et haec quoque propositio rursus identica est, et utrimque statum rei nominat in sua praesentia. Tertia explicatione miscetur uterque status, ut sensus sit Deum efficere posse, ut qui modus sit quanti in ipsius potentia, idem sit ipsius in sese existendi modus: quae propositio neque identica est, neque probata, neque vera.

The first: that God contains in His potency so [p. 20] great a magnitude as He contains in His potency; and in this on both sides [utrimque] the same state of the thing in potency is designated, and it is an identical proposition [propositio identica]. The next explication is: that that quantity (if any such is) which as greatest can have existence from God in the nature of things, that [quantity] can exist greatest from Him; and this proposition too is again identical, and on both sides names the state of the thing in its presence [praesentia]. In the third explication each state is mixed, so that the sense is that God can bring it about [efficere] that what mode [modus] of a quantum [quanti] is in His potency, the same be its mode of existing in itself: which proposition is neither identical, nor proved, nor true.

Cum enim confusio sit potentiae propria, distinctio actus, necessum est aliquem modum habere quod est in potentia, qui in actu existens transferri nequaquam possit. Inde est quod hic quanti modus ut quolibet assignato semper sit aliud maius, in potentia reperiri possit, in rerum natura inveniri repugnet: manifesta enim est in eo modo indeterminatio quaedam, quae actu existenti repugnet.

For since confusion is proper to potency, distinction to act, it is necessary [necessum] that what is in potency have some mode which can by no means be transferred [so as to be] existing in act [in actu existens]. Hence it is that this mode of a quantum, that to whatever [one] is assigned there is always another greater, can be found [reperiri] in potency, [but] is repugnant to being found [inveniri] in the nature of things: for manifest in that mode is a certain indetermination, which would be repugnant to [a thing] existing in act.

Tu modo suppositis explicationibus pro assumptione vide quid inferri possit. Ex prima nihil efficitur neque enim subsumi potest, ponatur igitur. Cum enim non nisi de Dei potentia in illa explicatione agatur, iam positum est omne quod poni potest. Neque felicius ex proxima fit pro-[p. 21]gressus; cum enim subiiciendum erit τὸ ponatur igitur, excipiet respondens nihil esse ponendum, cum nulla sit talis quantitas: propositio siquidem identica terminorum unitatem annunciat, non autem aliquam existentiam. Nondum itaque asserta est aliqua magnitudo maxima quae sit possibilis. Superest tertia explicatio quae nisi primo veritatem aliquam continere declaretur, ex ea nihil solidi deduci poterit.

You now, the explications being supposed for the assumption [pro assumptione], see what can be inferred. From the first nothing is effected, for neither can [the clause] 'let it therefore be posited' be subsumed. For since in that explication there is treatment [agatur] of nothing but the potency of God, everything that can be posited is already posited. Nor more happily is progress made from the next [pro-[p. 21]gressus]; for when the [words] τὸ 'let it therefore be posited' will have to be subjoined [subiiciendum], the respondent [respondens] will take exception [excipiet] that nothing is to be posited, since there is no such quantity: for an identical proposition announces the unity of the terms [terminorum], not however any existence. Not yet therefore has any greatest magnitude been asserted which is possible. There remains the third explication, from which, unless it is first declared to contain some truth, nothing solid will be able to be deduced.
Nunc ad posteriorem Suasionem me accingo, et hoc primo concedo quod factu est impossibile, idem et intellectu esse. Infinitum autem explicate in aliquo intellectu esse, hoc pernego.

Now I gird myself for the latter Persuasion, and this first I concede, that what is impossible to be done [factu], the same is [so] also to be understood [intellectu]. But that the infinite is explicitly [explicate] in any understanding [intellectu], this I flatly deny [pernego].

Neque ignarus sum videri me tibi praeter id quod convenit loqui, nimium enim faciles sumus ut ignota nobis notorum paria vel certe similia existimemus. Inde est quod divinam cognitionem, et si quae est alia coelestium intelligentiarum, vel inviti, conditionibus nostrae scientiae vestiamus. Et nisi mens mihi laeva sit, in hoc cardine impugnationis tuae difficultas vertitur.

Nor am I ignorant that I seem to you to speak beyond that which is fitting; for we are too easy [faciles], so that we judge things unknown to us equal to, or at least similar to, things known. Hence it is that we clothe the divine cognition, and if there is any other [cognition] of the heavenly intelligences [intelligentiarum], even unwilling [vel inviti], with the conditions of our science [scientiae]. And unless my mind be left-handed [laeva], on this hinge [cardine] the difficulty of your attack turns.

Cum enim videas cognitionem nostram singulis quantitatis speciebus singulas notitias adaptare, tantumdem aut certe quid simile in divinis quoque suspicaris; non quod opinor te successionem vel divisionem scientem transferre velle, sed quod eam obiectorum explicationem transferas quae sine divisio-[p. 22]ne exerceri non possit.

For since you see that our cognition adapts single notices [notitias] to single species of quantity, you suspect as much, or at least something similar, in divine [things] also; not that, I think, you knowingly [scientem] wish to transfer succession or division, but that you transfer that explication [explicationem] of objects which cannot be exercised without divisi-[p. 22]on.

Hoc itaque primo decretum volo non singulis obiectorum speciebus singulatim expressam deberi in substantiarum abstractarum intellectu imaginem, sed mira unitate ita naturam earum singulatim exprimi: ut una non plures modo, sed et infinitae comprehendantur.

This therefore I wish first [to be] decreed: that not to the single species of objects singly [singulatim] is an expressed image owed in the understanding of abstract substances [substantiarum abstractarum], but that by a wonderful unity their nature is so expressed singly [singulatim] that by one [image] not more [plures] only, but even infinite [species] are comprehended.

Si enim superficiei infinitas lineas comprehendere, corpori superficies sine numero excedere concedatur, et eo quidem modo, ut nulla superficies, nulla linea actu inexistat: Quanto magis spiritualibus corporea sine diserta expressione in sese continere et ea valere permittendum est?

For if it is granted to a surface to comprehend infinite lines, to a body to exceed surfaces without number, and indeed in such a way that no surface, no line, is in [it] [inexistat] in act: How much more is it to be permitted to spiritual [things] to contain in themselves corporeal [things] without distinct [diserta] expression, and to be equivalent to [valere] them?

Quod autem singulorum expressio, imagines non sint, inde manifestum est, quod multitudo quaelibet, et non sola materialis infinitati repugnare, ab iis quibus id otii est, facillime demonstrari possit. Quoniam itaque nota est nobis multitudinis ratio, ab hac ad negandum impossibilem in secretis substantiis modum arguere fas est. Quantumvis e diverso, ex modo in iis ignoto contra notas nobis naturas disputare sine illata Dialecticis dogmatibus violentia non sit permissum.

But that there is not an expression of singulars, [that is,] images, is manifest from this, that any multitude whatever, and not only a material [one], [is] repugnant to infinity [can]—by those who have leisure [otii] for it—most easily be demonstrated. Since therefore the reason [ratio] of multitude is known to us, it is lawful [fas est] to argue from this to denying an impossible mode in the secret [secretis] substances. However much [quantumvis], conversely [e diverso], to dispute from a mode unknown in them against natures known to us would not be permitted without violence brought upon [illata] the Dialectical dogmas.

Age modo, postquam hoc sanctum est, non esse disertas in intelligentiis singulorum materialium expressiones; ad ea quae obiecisti, collato pede, respondeamus. Argui infinitas species quantitatis cognosci, quia scilicet omnes cognoscun-[p. 23]tur, omnes vero multitudinem sine fine, limiteve significat, et per consequens infinitas.

Come now, after this has been sanctioned [sanctum est], that there are not distinct [disertas] expressions of single material [things] in the intelligences; let us respond to those things which you objected, foot set against foot [collato pede]. It was argued [argui] that infinite species of quantity are known, because, namely, all are known, [p. 23] but 'all' signifies a multitude without end or limit, and by consequence infinite [species].

[Header misprinted 'de mundi Mundi' for 'de materia Mundi'.] Ast ego te de iis quae sunt in potentia tanquam actu sint, proloqui, et quod consequens est, praeter modum et veritatem rei diserte pronuncio. Si enim aliqua actu sint et sine termino; ego et omnia et infinita ea esse confido: habent enim conditionem harum vocum et notitiarum capacem, et τὸ esse sine fine et limite infinitatem, in subiecto ut loquuntur capaci ex necessitate, sive infert, sive constituit.

But I expressly [diserte] declare that you speak out [proloqui] about those things which are in potency as though they were in act, and, what is consequent, beyond the mode and truth of the thing. For if some [things] are in act and without term [termino], I too trust that they are both all and infinite: for they have a condition capable of these words and notices [notitiarum], and τὸ 'to be without end and limit', in a capable subject [subiecto], as they say, of necessity either infers or constitutes infinity.

Si autem de iis loquaris quae in potentia sunt, in quibus vere et ipsa re nulla, multitudo est, quae (malum) importunitas est infinitatem conclusam arbitrari? Primo siquidem multitudinem et divisionem proba, et deinde caetera consequeris.

But if you speak about those things which are in potency, in which truly and in the thing itself [ipsa re] there is no multitude, what (plague take it! [malum]) importunity is it to judge infinity concluded? For first prove multitude and division, and then you will obtain [consequeris] the rest.

Ergone plura cognosci nego? non ego: sed ubi sit illa pluralitas interrogo. Obiecta si quidem non existunt, in intellectu perfecta est unitas; obiectiva existentia non rerum naturam sed nostram imaginationem sapit. Nusquam igitur aliqua realis est multitudo.

Do I then deny that more [things] [plura] are known? Not I: but I ask where that plurality is. If indeed the objects do not exist, in the understanding there is perfect unity; objective existence [obiectiva existentia] savours [sapit] not of the nature of things but of our imagination. Nowhere therefore is there any real multitude.

Et nunc puto superfluum ad singulas deductiones tuas privata responsa condere, postquam uno debellatum est congressu. Eodem siquidem spiritu interrogo ubi sint infinitae illae species? ubi multitudo colligenda? Ubi transitus infinitorum? ubi singulae finitae seu nulla non finita? Nihil horum [p. 24] actu existit, sed summa unitas et quieta per excessum entitativum, non transitum progressivum, denique super ea quae sunt in potentia, eminentia quaedam et exuperatio.

And now I think [it] superfluous to compose [condere] private [privata] responses to your single deductions, after the war has been finished [debellatum est] in one encounter [congressu]. For in the same spirit I ask: where are those infinite species? where the multitude to be gathered? Where the transit [transitus] of infinite [things]? where the single finite [ones], or none not finite? Nothing of these [p. 24] exists in act, but [there is] a supreme unity, and a quiet [one], through entitative [entitativum] excess, not progressive transit; finally, over those things which are in potency, a certain eminence and exuperance [exuperatio].

Asphal. Subverebar nescio quid, et Andabatae confidentia attonitus et disputationis subtilitate permotus; sed vicisti expectationem meam, Ereuni, et mundi pomoeria, iudice me, adamante et aere fortius stabilivisti, neque video in quo demonstratio tua Euclideae vel Archimedeae cuilibet quoad firmitatem cedat; sed etiam Geometricam potius quam Physicam agnosco, etsi de Physica materia procedat; Vulcania quoque retia {?qua} tam subtiliter texuerat Andabata, non tam exuisti quam rupisti et perscidisti.

Asphal. I was somewhat afraid [subverebar] of I know not what, both astonished by Andabata's confidence and deeply moved by the subtlety of the disputation; but you have conquered my expectation, Ereunius, and the pomoeria [pomoeria] of the world you have established, me being judge, more strongly than adamant and bronze; nor do I see in what your demonstration yields to any Euclidean or Archimedean [demonstration] as regards firmness; but I also recognize [it as] Geometrical rather than Physical, although it proceeds about Physical matter; the Vulcanian nets too, which [qua, read quae] Andabata had woven so subtly, you have not so much slipped out of [exuisti] as broken and cut through.

Unum est quod non tam incuso quam desidero, et est, quod nondum videris intentioni Andabatae fecisse satis. Si enim asserat stellas quidem infinitas esse, sed non spatiis realibus consutas, non video quid linearum interceptio ubi nullae erunt, officere possit, et tamen quae de Dei gloria et munificentia in genus humanum aggerenda producta sunt, eandem vim obtinere quam in continuitate mundi, mihi apparet. [Knot iii follows: Margin 'Nodus III. Non esse plures mundos.']

There is one [thing] which I do not so much accuse as miss [desidero], and it is, that you seem not yet to have satisfied the intention of Andabata. For if he should assert that the stars indeed are infinite, but not sewn together [consutas] by real spaces, I do not see what the interception [interceptio] of lines, where there will be none, could hinder [officere]; and yet the things which were brought forward about the glory and munificence of God towards the human race, to be heaped up [aggerenda], [it] appears to me [that they] obtain the same force as in the continuity of the world. [Knot iii follows: Margin 'Knot III. That there are not more worlds [than one].']

terms: In syllogistic, assumptio is the minor premise (the 'subsumption' under the major), and assumere is to state it; also simply 'take up'.
Ereunius' reply turns on which reading of Andabata's axiom can serve as the minor premise ('pro assumptione') and so let 'ponatur igitur' be subsumed.
To place a particular under a universal as the minor premise; subiicere = add underneath, put as subject.
Scholastic syllogistic; cf. 'quo singulare sub universali subsumitur' (the dictum de omni).
Scholastic technical term: 'nullum inconveniens sequitur' = no absurdity follows; the criterion of possibility Andabata takes from Aristotle (Metaph. IX.3, 1047a24–26; De caelo I.12).
a tautology; a proposition whose predicate repeats the subject.
White's point: an identical proposition asserts only the 'unity of the terms', not any existence.
The created quantity's two 'states': as contained in God's power, and as existing in itself.
Aristotelian; White adds that 'confusion is proper to potency, distinction to act', the ground of his denial of an actual infinite.
Scholastic 'mode of being'; 'praeter modum et veritatem rei' also plays on modus = due measure.
a thing having quantity, a quantity.

Two senses here: the three 'explications' (readings) of the axiom, and the 'explicit' (unfolded, part-by-part) presence of an object in an intellect, opposed to the 'complicated' unity of angelic knowledge (Cusan/Thomist complicatio–explicatio).
kind; or the intelligible species (form) by which a thing is known.
'species quantitatis' are kinds (sizes) of quantity; the related 'imago' and 'expressio' are the Thomist species impressa/expressa in the intellect.
Scholastic 'notitia' = act or item of knowledge.
angels; separated (immaterial) substances; secretae = separated, set apart (not 'hidden').
Thomist doctrine that angels know by few, more universal species (ST I q.55 a.3); White uses it to deny 'distinct' images of each material thing.
Of an expression in an intellect: separately articulated, one image per object.
Scholastic: parts that are only potentially 'in' the continuum do not 'inexist' in act (Aristotle's potential infinite of division).
be worth, have the force of, avail.
Spirits contain bodily things 'virtually', i.e. have their value without containing them formally.
existence as an object of thought (esse obiectivum), not existence in the thing.
Scholastic esse obiectivum = 'being in the intellect'; not modern 'objective'.
belonging to the being [entitas] of a thing, as opposed to its operation.
Scholastic; God's or the intelligence's 'excess' is in being, not by stepping through (transitus) the finite cases.
Scholastic 'eminent' containment: the higher contains the lower in a higher way (cf. ps.-Dionysius).
traverse, go through one by one.
Aristotle (Phys. III, VI): the infinite cannot be traversed (diexelthein); Ereunius denies there is any 'transit' in the intelligences.
the business has been made out
Andabata repeats Ereunius' 'confectum profecto est' from the end of part 1.
White calls Andabata's two proofs 'suasiones' (persuasions), implying they are not demonstrations.
τὸ (τὸ ponatur igitur; τὸ esse sine fine)
Greek article used to nominalise a phrase.
Humanist-scholastic habit of quoting a phrase as a noun with the Greek article.
foot set against foot / fight out at close quarters
Military idiom from Livy and Caesar ('collato pede'), for answering point by point.
unless I am mistaken; laevus = left, unlucky, foolish.
Echo of Virgil, Aen. II.54 and Ecl. I.16 'si mens non laeva fuisset'.
Colloquial in Plautus, Terence and Cicero ('quae, malum, est ista ...').
the sacred boundary of a city (Rome).
Classical metaphor: Ereunius has fixed the world's boundaries.
more strongly than adamant and bronze
Echo of Horace, Odes III.30.1 'aere perennius'.
the fine net in which Vulcan caught Mars and Venus.
Homer, Od. VIII.266–366; Ovid, Met. IV.176–189: a proverbial subtle snare.
Stars 'not sewn together by real spaces': infinitely many stars without an infinite real distance between them.
the cutting off, enclosing of lines between points.
Refers to Ereunius' argument in part 1 that any two determinate parts enclose a finite line.
notes: Unit: Dialogue I, Knot ii, part 2 of 2. PDF pp. 28–35 = printed pp. 17–24. It starts on p. 17 at Andabata's 'Non tam facile quam credis confectum est negotium', where the margin has 'Argumenta pro infinito solvuntur' (printed 'Argu-menta pro in-finito soluun-tur'). It ends with Asphalius' speech '…mihi apparet' on p. 24. Below it, Ereunius' 'Etsi non credam Andabatam de hac re negotium mihi facessere velle' begins Knot iii, with the margin 'Nodus III. Non esse plures mundos' (FM2's table: iii. Mundos non esse plures, p. 24). The offset of +11 holds (p. 24 = PDF 35).
Rows: one row per speech. The long speeches of Andabata and Ereunius are split at sentence breaks so that Latin and English line up. Printed page breaks are marked [p. n].

Conventions as in glossary.md: long s → s; æ/œ → ae/oe; tildes expanded (cōtendo → contendo, quātam → quantam, nō → non, inconueniēs → inconveniens); consonantal u → v; accents dropped. 'otî' (p. 22) → otii; 'i.' and 'v.g.' kept and expanded in brackets. Spellings kept as printed: 'arenae', 'necessum', 'exurgunt', 'annunciat', 'pronuncio', 'caetera', 'expectationem', 'coelestium'. The Greek article τὸ (pp. 21, 23) is kept.

Printed oddities: (a) p. 17, 'Sed talis quantitatis posita evidenter est infinita': the genitive has no head noun; translated '[the magnitude] of such a quantity, posited'. It may be a misprint for 'talis quantitas posita'. (b) p. 19, 'periturus' ('about to perish') makes no sense; read as 'petiturus' ('about to seek'), a likely misprint (r for t). (c) p. 19, 'quantum maximam' where p. 17 has 'quantam maximam'; kept as printed. (d) p. 18, 'intelligit' (singular) with 'Deus, et si quae creaturae', then 'intelligunt' (plural); kept. (e) p. 23 running head 'de mundi Mundi' is a misprint for 'de materia Mundi'. (f) p. 24, 'retia qua' is read as 'quae' (the ligature or the e is probably missing); marked {?qua}.

Sense notes: (a) p. 22, 'Argui …' at the start of a sentence is taken as a historic infinitive ('It was argued'), summing up Andabata's argument; it may be a misprint for 'Arguis' or 'Arguisti'. (b) p. 22, 'Quantumvis e diverso … non sit permissum' is read as a concessive contrast ('however much …, conversely … would not be permitted'): you may argue from known natures to unknown, but not from unknown modes against known natures. (c) p. 22, the sentence 'quod multitudo quaelibet … infinitati repugnare … demonstrari possit' has an accusative-infinitive inside a 'quod' clause; the English keeps the order with dashes. (d) p. 18, the dative 'singulis finitis maiorem' / 'omnibus finitis aliquam maiorem' is a dative of comparison (= 'than'), which is unusual; the English gives 'than' and notes the dative. (e) p. 21, 'neque enim subsumi potest, ponatur igitur': 'ponatur igitur' (Andabata's minor premise) is the subject of 'subsumi'; '[the clause]' is supplied.
Uncertain: {?qua} (p. 24, read quae); 'periturus' (p. 19, read petiturus); 'Argui' (p. 22). The reading 'consutas' (p. 24, not 'confusas') was confirmed on a 300 dpi crop. No illegible words.

Verification pass: the transcription was compared again with the page images, and the English with the Latin, sentence by sentence (cases, tenses, moods, negatives, comparatives, omissions). This gave 4 corrections: (1) p. 18, 'singulis itaque finitis maiorem cognoscunt' had been rendered 'to each finite one'; changed to 'than each [singulis, dative]' with a note, since the comparison is the point. (2) p. 21, 'poterit' (future) had been rendered 'can'; corrected to 'will be able'. (3) p. 19, 'quam admiranda magis quam investiganda' had been rendered 'how [much] to be admired rather than to be investigated', which blurred the comparative 'magis … quam'; corrected to 'how much more to be admired than to be investigated'. (4) p. 24, 'eandem vim obtinere … mihi apparet' had made 'the things … brought forward' the subject of 'appear'; the accusative-infinitive depends on 'apparet', so the English now reads '[it] appears to me [that they] obtain the same force'.
